title: Episode 321: James II & VII: The Glorious Revolution of 1688 and the Battle of the Boyne
description:
The dramatic, tragic reign of King James II of England and VII of Scotland. A courageous naval hero at the Battle of Lowestoft, James succeeded his brother Charles II in 1685 with goodwill, swiftly crushing the Monmouth Rebellion with brutal 'Bloody Assizes'. But James's unyielding, authoritarian determination to re-Catholicize England alienated the Church, the judiciary, and Parliament. When his young Catholic queen gave birth to an unexpected male heir in June 1688, sparking rumors of a baby smuggled in a warming pan, English Protestant peers invited William of Orange to invade. In the bloodless 'Glorious Revolution', James's army deserted him, and he fled to France, throwing the Great Seal into the Thames. Defeated at the Battle of the Boyne in 1690, discover the last Catholic king of Great Britain.

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, our Kings and Queens of England series examines the sovereign whose unbending religious zeal sparked a revolution that birthed modern constitutional democracy: the last Catholic monarch of Britain, King James II. Here is George with the dramatic story of 1688 and the Battle of the Boyne.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE LORD HIGH ADMIRAL: NAVAL GLORY AND CONVERSION: 1633 TO 1685
Born in October 1633 at St. James's Palace, James Stuart, Duke of York, was endowed with personal bravery, rigorous administrative diligence, and a stiff, humorless obstinacy that stood in stark contrast to his charming brother Charles II. Escaping parliamentary captivity during the Civil War disguised as a girl, James served with distinction as a professional cavalry officer under the French marshal Turenne. Following the Restoration in 1660, James served for thirteen years as Lord High Admiral of the Royal Navy, demonstrating personal courage at sea during the Second and Third Anglo-Dutch Wars, commanding the fleet in the thick of battle at Lowestoft in 1665 and Solebay in 1672. But in the late 1660s, James secretly converted to Roman Catholicism. When Parliament passed the Test Act in 1673, James refused to take the Anglican sacrament, resigning his naval command and marrying the fifteen-year-old Italian Catholic princess Mary of Modena. Surviving the virulent hysteria of the Exclusion Crisis under his brother's protection, James ascended the throne peacefully in February 1685, with the realm initially trusting his promise to defend the Church of England. James's naval career was characterized by conspicuous personal courage and meticulous organizational diligence. As Lord High Admiral, he modernized the naval administration, codified fighting instructions for fleet line-of-battle tactics, and championed the development of naval dockyards at Chatham and Portsmouth. At the Battle of Solebay in 1672, when his flagship the Royal Prince was disabled by Dutch cannon fire, James transferred his flag to the St. Michael under heavy fire, and when that vessel was battered, transferred again to the London, earning the fierce devotion of ordinary sailors who affectionately nicknamed him 'Old Rowley's brother'.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: MONMOUTH'S REBELLION AND THE BLOODY ASSIZES: 1685
James's reign was immediately challenged in June 1685 by the Monmouth Rebellion. Charles II's illegitimate Protestant son, James Scott, Duke of Monmouth, landed at Lyme Regis in Dorset with eighty men, proclaiming himself rightful king. Thousands of West Country clothworkers, miners, and yeomen flocked to his standard, armed with scythes and pitchforks. On July 6, 1685, at the Battle of Sedgemoor in Somerset—the last pitched battle fought on English soil—James's regular army under the Earl of Feversham and John Churchill routed the rebel pikemen in a nocturnal fog. Monmouth was captured hiding in a ditch and beheaded on Tower Hill in a gruesome execution that took five blows of the ax. James unleashed terrifying judicial vengeance: under the ruthless Lord Chief Justice George Jeffreys, the 'Bloody Assizes' toured the West Country, sentencing over three hundred rebels to be hanged, drawn, and quartered, their boiled heads and limbs impaled on crossroads across Somerset, while eight hundred more were transported into slavery in Barbados, horrifying the English nation. Monmouth's rebellion was a tragic tragedy of errors: Monmouth was a charismatic, handsome figure who claimed that Charles II had secretly married his mother Lucy Walter, promising a return to Protestant liberty. But his poorly armed rebel army of West Country rustics was easily outmatched by the regular soldiers of the Royal Army at Sedgemoor. The subsequent Bloody Assizes under Judge Jeffreys horrified even royalists: Jeffreys roared at trembling prisoners from the bench, sentencing men to be hanged in batches and displaying their tarred corpses across western villages, fostering a deep, bitter hatred for James's regime that exploded three years later.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE JESUIT IN THE CLOSET: THE ASSAULT ON ENGLISH LAW: 1686 TO 1688
Emboldened by his victory over Monmouth, James made the fatal assumption that his subjects would meekly submit to his royal will. He expanded his standing army to thirty thousand men, quartering troops on Hounslow Heath to intimidate London, and placed Catholic officers in command in defiance of the Test Act. In 1687, James issued the Declaration of Indulgence, using his royal 'dispensing power' to unilaterally suspend all penal laws against Catholics and dissenters. When the fellows of Magdalen College, Oxford, refused to elect a royal Catholic nominee as their president, James expelled them by force, converting the college into a Catholic seminary. He appointed Jesuit father Edward Petre to the Privy Council and welcomed a papal nuncio to Windsor. James believed he was championing enlightened religious tolerance; his subjects, however, watching Louis XIV's brutal dragonnades persecuting Huguenots across the Channel following the Revocation of the Edict of Nantes, viewed James's actions as a tyrannical conspiracy to impose French-style Catholic absolutism. James's assault on English universities and corporations was a catastrophic political blunder. By forcing Catholic fellows into Oxford colleges and dismissing Anglican justices of the peace and deputy lieutenants who refused to support the repeal of the Test Acts, James alienated the natural bedrock of Stuart monarchy: the Tory country gentry and the Church of England clergy. When he appointed the Jesuit priest Father Edward Petre to his Privy Council, moderate English Catholics like Lord Belasyse warned the king that his reckless speed was driving his Protestant subjects into armed rebellion, but James stubbornly insisted that concession was the path to abdication.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE SEVEN BISHOPS AND THE WARMING PAN BABY: JUNE 1688
In May 1688, James made a catastrophic miscalculation: he ordered all Anglican clergy to read his Declaration of Indulgence aloud from their pulpits during Sunday service. Seven prominent bishops, led by Archbishop of Canterbury William Sancroft, submitted a polite, respectful petition questioning the king's legal dispensing power. James flew into a rage, accusing the bishops of seditious rebellion and locking them in the Tower of London. When the Seven Bishops were tried in Westminster Hall in June, the jury delivered a verdict of Not Guilty, prompting wild, thunderous cheering across London and celebrations among the soldiers at Hounslow Heath. Two days later, an explosive event altered the dynastic landscape: Queen Mary of Modena gave birth to a healthy son, Prince James Francis Edward Stuart. Until that moment, English Protestants had tolerated James, knowing his heirs were his Protestant daughters Mary and Anne. Now, a permanent Catholic dynasty was born. Panicked Protestants circulated a sensational conspiracy theory that the queen had suffered a miscarriage and that a strange baby had been smuggled into the bed in a brass warming pan. The trial of the Seven Bishops in Westminster Hall was the moral climax of the reign. Crowds of thousands knelt in the streets outside the hall to receive the blessings of the bishops as they were escorted to and from the Tower. When the jury returned a verdict of acquittal after an all-night deliberation, church bells rang across London, bonfires blazed, and an effigy of the Pope was publicly burned in Cheapside. When the news reached James at his military camp on Hounslow Heath, the king heard his own soldiers cheering hysterically. When James asked what the cheering was for, an officer replied: 'Nothing, sire, but the soldiers rejoicing that the bishops are acquitted.' James grimly murmured: 'Do you call that nothing?'

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE INVITATION AND THE GLORIOUS REVOLUTION: NOVEMBER 1688
On June 30, 1688, the day the Seven Bishops were acquitted, seven prominent English statesmen—the 'Immortal Seven', representing both Whig and Tory factions—dispatched a secret, coded letter to William of Orange, Stadtholder of the Dutch Republic and husband to James's eldest Protestant daughter Mary. They invited William to invade England with an army to restore English liberties and investigate the legitimacy of the royal infant. On November 5, 1688—the anniversary of the Gunpowder Plot—William's armada of four hundred ships landed at Torbay in Devon under the banner: 'The Protestant Religion and the Liberties of England'. James marched to Salisbury to confront the invader with his superior army. But James's spirit collapsed: plagued by severe nosebleeds and paranoia, he watched his commanders desert him one by one, including his favored general John Churchill and his own younger daughter, Princess Anne. Returning broken-hearted to London, James threw the Great Seal of England into the River Thames and attempted to flee, being caught by Kentish fishermen before William arranged for his discreet escape to France. William of Orange's invasion fleet of November 1688 was an amphibious armada of colossal proportions: four hundred transport ships escorted by fifty Dutch men-of-war, carrying fourteen thousand veteran soldiers, twenty-one thousand horses, and modern artillery. As William landed at Brixham in Torbay, James's army at Salisbury began disintegrating. Lord Churchill, whom James had raised from obscurity to wealth and title, deserted to William in the middle of the night. Princess Anne slipped out of Whitehall Palace in a hackney coach to join the rebels in Nottingham. When James learned his own daughter had turned against him, the broken father wept: 'God help me! Even my children have forsaken me!'

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE BATTLE OF THE BOYNE: JULY 1, 1690
Welcomed at Versailles by Louis XIV with a luxurious palace at Saint-Germain-en-Laye, James refused to abandon his claim to the throne. In March 1689, backed by French gold and officers, James landed in Ireland, where the Catholic majority rallied to him as their legitimate sovereign. The Protestant garrison of Derry shut its gates against James's army, with apprentice boys shouting 'No Surrender!', enduring a horrific one-hundred-and-five-day siege in which citizens ate rats and tallow before being relieved. On July 1, 1690, King William III and King James II faced each other across the River Boyne near Drogheda in one of the most consequential battles in European history. William, wounded in the shoulder by a cannonball on the eve of battle, led his multinational army of thirty-six thousand men across the river, shattering James's Franco-Irish cavalry and infantry. James watched the defeat from a nearby hill, panicked, and fled the field, riding through the night to Dublin and sailing for France, earning the bitter Gaelic nickname 'Séamas an Chaca'—'James the Coward'. The Battle of the Boyne on July 1, 1690, pitted the two monarchs directly against each other for the crowns of Britain and Ireland. William, wearing an orange sash and commanding an elite multinational coalition of Dutch, Danish, Huguenot, and English troops, personally led his cavalry across the chest-deep waters of the Boyne under heavy musketry fire. James's Irish cavalry under Patrick Sarsfield fought with desperate bravery, but his ill-trained infantry was broken. When James fled to Dublin before the battle was fully concluded, he told Lady Tyrconnell that her countrymen had run away, to which the witty Irish noblewoman famously retorted: 'I see that your Majesty hath won the race!' James sailed for France, never to return.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE SAINTLY EXILE OF SAINT-GERMAIN: 1701
James spent the final decade of his life at Saint-Germain-en-Laye in profound, ascetic penance. Convinced that his loss of three kingdoms was God's righteous punishment for his youthful sins of the flesh, James wore an iron chain around his waist, scourged his back with whips, and spent hours kneeling in prayer before the Blessed Sacrament alongside Trappist monks. In 1692, the destruction of the French invasion fleet by the Anglo-Dutch navy at the Battle of La Hogue extinguished his last hope of a military return. In England, the Convention Parliament had declared that James had abdicated by throwing the Great Seal into the Thames and fleeing, enacting the Bill of Rights and the Toleration Act, permanently establishing parliamentary supremacy. On September 16, 1701, sixty-seven-year-old James II died of a brain hemorrhage at Saint-Germain. On his deathbed, he urged his thirteen-year-old son, the 'Old Pretender', never to abandon his Catholic faith for the crowns of the world, passing the torch of Jacobite rebellion to the next century. In his final years at Saint-Germain-en-Laye, James lived as a saintly penitent, writing touching spiritual advice for his young son James Francis Edward Stuart. He fasted rigorously, washed the feet of poor men during Holy Week, and sought absolute spiritual forgiveness for his political failures. When he died in September 1701, King Louis XIV of France visited his deathbed and promised to recognize his son as King James III of England and VIII of Scotland, igniting sixty years of Jacobite rebellions that would culminate on the bloody moor of Culloden in 1746.
